Back to backwardation 
• 
LME warehouse stocks remain tight, particularly after the record level of warrant cancellations on 20th 
April.  This has helped to drive the LME cash price higher than 3-month since mid-March, marking the 
deepest and most sustained period of backwardation since mid-2008.    
• 
In our conversations with market participants during CESCO week in Santiago two weeks ago, we 
found a general consensus that Chinese demand in H1 has been disappointing, but most people we met 
are expecting a rebound in H2.  Production concerns remain at the forefront, with Q1 output again 
seeing various disruptions. 
• 
The copper price was subdued in early April as global economic data depressed sentiments but the 
latter half of the month saw a resurgence, driven higher by the short-covering rally.

Low stocks outside China drive LME backwardation 
Having remained in contango for over a year, LME copper 
cash and 3-month prices moved into backwardation in mid-
March and continued to plunge deeper in April, with the back 
reaching over -$152/t by the end of the month.  This is the 
largest one-day backwardation value seen since August 2008, 
and the deepest sustained move into backwardation since mid-
2008. Just before the 2008 crisis broke, supply was severely 
disrupted by a number of mine strikes and stocks were low, 
meaning concerns about the immediate availability of metal 
kept the market in backwardation. As the crisis resulted in an 
increase in availability of prompt material, the forward curve 
moved into contango throughout by year-end. This time 
around, we are seeing some degree of supply disruption, but 
not to the same extent as in Q2 2008.  It is the extremely low 
levels of exchange stocks in the world outside China, 
contrasting with the high inventory levels known to exist 
inside it, that has made the backwardation we are seeing today possible.   
We believe that the underlying reason behind the disparity in stock levels has been that a lot of material is 
fundamentally in the wrong location, as Western demand was not as depressed as many had initially 
feared while Chinese demand has so far turned out to be much lower than most people’s expectations for 
this year.  However, the tightness seen outside China has been exacerbated by the high levels of warrant 
cancellations in LME warehouses in the last few months.  While some of this material may have gone 
into China, trade data indicate that most of it could not have done.  The cancellation levels have also been 
too high for the remaining material to have been consumed, and so it seems likely that much of the 
material has gone or is destined to go into private warehouses.  The high levels of cancellations have also 
created short term scarcity of physical metal, as queues have lengthened to deliver metal out of LME 
warehouses.  This drives up spot cathode premia and prices for prompt delivery, resulting in the 
backwardation we are seeing.  It is not clear whether the backwardation is side-effect of a drive amongst 
certain market players to boost premia, or the desired result:  Physical scarcity boosts premia, thus 
benefiting anyone holding copper cathode.  A backwardation can also benefit a holder of metal, as they 
can lend it to the market by selling cash and buying it back further forward.  Realistically, it is probably a 
combination of both. 
In the last month, the level of cancelled warrants in LME warehouses was declining as material cancelled 
earlier was delivered out.  However, a sudden raft of cancellations in warehouses around the world on 20th 
April moved over 40,000t off-warrant, boosting the LME cash price and driving a wider backwardation 
situation.   This global inventory cancellation which affected six warehouse locations in five countries

was the biggest one-day change ever, and happened to occur on the Friday following the copper market’s 
annual CESCO week get-together and CRU conference in Santiago. 
Copper price falters and rebounds in April 
The copper price moved down in the first half of April, having 
held in a relatively narrow band of $8,200-8,700/t since late 
January, due to worries over the global economy and Chinese 
demand.  European debt concerns flared up again, with a 
disappointing debt auction by the Spanish government and the 
release of gloomy retail and business activity data for February, 
while the US outlook cooled on lower than expected jobs 
growth data and the failure of the Federal Reserve to announce 
another stimulus package.  Further downward pressure was 
applied to the price by the increasing apprehension in the 
market over Chinese demand growth prospects for 2012.  
Indeed, in our conversations with market participants during 
CESCO week, the general consensus was of weaker than 
expected demand in China in Q2.  If we compare the five-day 
moving averages of open interest against the cash price on the 
LME during mid-April (see accompanying chart), the falling price coupled with net reductions in open 
positions indicate a tendency towards liquidation of long positions at that time.  
However, prices steadied during CESCO week as market players found themselves in broad agreement 
over a resurgence of Chinese demand in H2, while weaker preliminary Q1 supply data bolstered support.  
The simultaneous warrant cancellations on 20th April, discussed above, squeezed near-term availability 
outside China during the following week.  With open interest falling at the same time, it appears that the 
squeeze has precipitated a round of short covering, which kick-started a rebound in prices.  
China stock build eases 
In the face of a weaker than expected start to the year, many are questioning the outlook Chinese demand 
in 2012.  That stock levels are very high is not disputed, and stories abound of idled mills and reduced 
orders for cathode from Chinese semi-fabricators.  While many believe that around 80-90% of the 
estimated 600,000t of stocks in Shanghai bonded warehouses are being utilised for financing purposes, 
there are still numerous signs that stocks are too high for physical requirements.  A number of exporters 
of cathode to China tell us that they have received requests from customers to delay shipments, and there 
have been incidences of material headed for China being diverted to Europe.  The significant negative 
arbitrage between LME and SHFE has encouraged a few traders to engage in re-exporting cathode to 
Asian LME warehouses, and earlier this week, a number of Chinese smelters including Jiangxi Copper 
announced a joint agreement to deliver cathode to the LME over the next two months, ostensibly to ease 
tightness in the global market.  (We note that this is only possible due to the tolling regulations introduced

However, the course of the Chinese market is beginning to turn.  Consumption is set to pick up in Q2 by 
around 13%, mainly due to seasonal working patterns.  We understand that many of the semi-fabricators 
have only booked 60% of their annual requirements, implying that they will have to enter the spot market 
at some point, supporting demand.  From a macroeconomic perspective, China’s latest official 
manufacturing PMI showed a reading of 53.3 for April, up from 53.1 in March, which, if not 
overwhelmingly bullish, is positive for growth prospects.   Finally, stock levels have begun to stabilise: 
Last week’s SHFE total of just under 205,000t represented a decline of 9.9% from the peak of 227,000t 
on 16th March.  Moreover, we are informed that the build-up in bonded stocks has slowed. 
In our last Monitor, we wrote that Chinese refined imports would decline in March due to increased 
domestic production, mediocre consumption, high bonded stocks and low premia, and imports did fall by 
8% to just under 345,000t.  This gives total first quarter imports at a record level of 1.06Mt – an increase 
of just 1.1% compared to the previous quarter, but a massive 78.6% increase compared to Q1 2011.  
So, despite the second consecutive record quarterly cathode imports and a slight increase in production so 
far this year, it appears that the stock build ran out of steam in April.  We therefore believe that the 
expected pickup in consumption in Q2 is beginning to materialise.  Looking ahead, while bonded stocks 
remain at high levels, the unfavourable SHFE/LME arbitrage will continue to discourage spot import 
activity, and following our expectations that consumption will grow by more than production, stocks 
should begin to be drawn down.  
Early Q1 supply data down 
Q1 supply results are beginning to come in, and the details of a 
number of disruptions have been revealed.  CRU production 
forecasts already take into account the higher likelihood of 
weather-related disturbances in Q1, due to the occurrence of the 
rainy season in Queensland, the African Copperbelt and the 
Atacama desert in Chile and Peru, as well as winter in the 
northern hemisphere.  Chinese output is expected to be 
disrupted at all points of the supply chain due to the New Year 
holiday.  We also note that Q1 is the start of the calendar year, 
and the quarter which - in many cases - inspires the least 
consideration amongst workers for annual production targets.  
At this stage, we know that heavy rains disrupted the Collahuasi 
and Tintaya mines, technical problems beset at least three 
smelters causing outages, and ore grades were lower than 
expected at Bingham Canyon.  Labour troubles persisted at

Grasberg and flared up at Kansanshi and a few other, smaller Zambian operations, reducing output at 
these mines too.  However, ramping up continues at the Los Bronces and Antamina brownfield expansion 
projects, offsetting some of the production losses elsewhere.  
Given the above, we see refined output amounting to around 4.7Mt in the first quarter of the year, down 
4.4% compared to the previous quarter and almost 0.6% higher than a year earlier.  Output is expected to 
pick up from Q2 as extreme weather conditions recede and as Chinese productivity improves following 
its holiday-interrupted first quarter.  However, output growth is not expected to come close to meeting 
consumption increases in Q2, so our refined deficit is projected to grow from around 20,000t in Q1 to 
330,000t in Q2, with much of the latter expected to be met by the drawdown in Chinese stocks.  In H2, 
we see flat production growth in Q3 and an increase in Q4, as mine, smelter and refinery workers push to 
meet calendar year targets. 
Al rod market tightness shows 
In our February monitor, we observed that the recent closures of aluminium production units, mainly due 
to low prices and oversupply, would lead to a shortage of aluminium rod.  We are beginning to see 
evidence of this: Recent media reports quote US wire and cable producers as saying that they have been 
forced to increase expenditure by sourcing rod outside the US, due to two smelter outages in the country, 
and imports of aluminium rod, bar and profile were up 25% y-o-y in February into the US.    
While we have yet to hear that the wire and cable plants have turned to copper rod as a substitute due to 
the scarcity of aluminium rod, it remains a possibility if the situation persists.  At the very least this 
reduces the possibility of substitution losses from copper rod to aluminium.  
Price testing downside support 
The uncertain start to April saw the 3-month LME price test but 
fail to break below the short term uptrend line of $7,900/t, after 
which it seems that short-covering has driven the price rebound 
seen in recent days.  While the squeeze on LME stocks has 
exerted more upward pressure on the cash price, driving the 
backwardation, the 3-month price has also moved up strongly, 
implying underlying support for prices above $8,000/t.  As the 
chart indicates, the 3-month price has recently breached the 
100-day and now the 30-day moving averages.  At the time of 
going to press, the price had approached and retreated from 
$8,400 and was looking ready to test $8,200/t on the way down.  
If this level is breached we would expect the next test to be at 
$7,900/t, where we anticipate firm support as stocks are drawn 
down and sentiments improve as evidence of higher seasonal 
demand materialises.

Consumption trends 
Chinese copper wirerod market slows 
Consumption of copper wirerod in China grew by a modest 
5.4% y-o-y in Q1 2012, reaching 1.323Mt.  We attribute 
the slowing growth primarily to subdued domestic demand 
throughout Q1, as semi-fabricators reported low capacity 
utilisation due to a drop in order rates.  This occurred 
through multiple product segments, as demand for building 
wire was weak due to slowing housing construction and 
demand for appliance wiring was also subdued by high 
finished-product inventories.  Nevertheless, growth in 
China remains supported by the social housing project, 
which received a budget increase in March, as the 
government hopes to complete 5M homes in 2012 alone.  
We were told by wire and cable producers that the 
economic slowdown in 2011 began to affect their 
operations.  The rates of growth in China’s GDP and IP 
slowed in 2011 and are expected to decline further in 2012, 
which should impact the wirerod industry gradually.  In addition, building wire demand was subdued, as it was 
affected by the severe macro controls applied to the property market.  One large sized wire and cable producer 
reported that its capacity utilisation is about 60% at the moment, compared to running at full capacity last year.  
The difficulty it faces currently is that it is short of new orders, which are only one third the level of the same 
period last year. 
The difficulties in the Chinese wirerod market were strongly felt in North East Asia in Q1 2012, where 
production of copper wirerod shrank by 3.7% y-o-y in the period.  South Korea was the region most severely 
affected, with production falling by 7.8% y-o-y, whereas, Taiwan recorded a 3.7% decline.  It was also reported 
that wire and cable production in Vietnam fell by 19.1%.  Production in Japan remained largely flat, supported 
by a rebounding domestic construction sector and strong industrial growth.  However, much of this growth was 
due to the weak conditions in the comparable period in 2011, following the natural disasters that struck in 
March 2011.  
Chinese production of wirerod increased to 1.265Mt in Q1 2012, up by 5.2% y-o-y.  There have been few 
announcements of new projects coming on in the region.  The only major development in the past three months 
is the beginning of construction work at Wuxi Lineo Science and Technology Group’s 60,000t/y copper 
wirerod mill in Jiangsu province.  Start-up is expected to take place by October 2012.  The company will also 
invest in a second phase expansion project that will involve the addition of another 60,000t/y wirerod 
production line by November 2014.  The plant will be primarily fed with refined copper cathode sourced from 
Tongling Nonferrous Metals in Anhui province and is designed to serve domestic wire and cable producers

Renewed optimism in the Americas 
Consumption of copper wirerod in the US strengthened in 
Q1 2012, growing by 2.7% y-o-y to 327,000t.  This 
compares to a decline of 0.2% in Q1 2011.  Although 
business conditions remain difficult in the US due to the 
depressed construction sector, the negative trend for housing 
permits appears to have stabilised at a low level and is not 
expected to decline further.  Meanwhile, the automotive 
sector is performing well and is supporting copper wirerod 
consumption, which has further benefitted from a return of 
consumer confidence and demand from the industrial 
sectors.   
US production of copper wirerod also increased in Q1 2012, 
rising by 2.8% to 342,000t.  This is set to grow further in the 
imminent future with the expected commissioning of SDI 
LaFarga LLC’s 82,000t/y copper wirerod plant in New 
Haven, Indiana, this month.  The plant is expected to reach 70% utilisation before the end of 2012.  The joint 
venture company involves the merged interests of US-based carbon steel producer and scrap metal recycler, 
Steel Dynamic’s Inc. and Spain-based copper semis fabricator, LaFarga Group.  The facility will consume 
copper scrap in its production process, with the majority likely to consist of No.  2 copper scrap from Steel 
Dynamic’s scrap processing facility, OmniSource Corp.  The use of anything other than the highest grade 
copper scrap is unprecedented in the US wirerod market and SDI LaFarga’s facility will therefore function as a 
unique new area of demand for No.  2 copper scrap in the US.  This will decrease the availability of US No.  2 
scrap for export to China and should narrow scrap discounts. 
We have also seen promising signs of growth in the Brazilian wirerod sector, with consumption of copper 
wirerod increasing by 2.4% y-o-y in Q1 2012.  Much of the growth came from the government’s reduction to 
its inflation-mitigating interest rates, which encouraged economic growth.  Our forecast for Brazilian cathode 
consumption in 2012 is for a rise of 6% y-o-y, outperforming the increase in industrial production due to 
copper demand’s heavy exposure to essential infrastructure developments related to the 2014 World Cup 
hosted in Brazil.  Moreover, production of copper wirerod rose by 19.6% in the same period, marking the 
region as a net producer of the material.  Previously, shortages in domestic production were made up through

Russia’s transition to wirerod exports plateaus 
We estimate that Russian copper wirerod production rose 
by 213,000t or 44% y-o-y to reach 698,000t in 2011 on the 
back of export duties on cathode imposed in November 
2010.  The production increase in Q1 2012 was, however, 
less marked, as we believe that the transition from cathode 
exports to copper wirerod exports was nearing completion 
by the end of 2011.  Nonetheless, Russkaya Mednaya 
Kompaniya’s (RMK) Kyshtym Electrolytic Copper 
wirerod plant (JSC ‘KMEZ’) in the Chelyabinsk region is 
undergoing development and modernisation work, which 
involved an investment of 144M roubles (US$4.8M) in 
2011 and is expected to require at least a further 170M 
roubles (US$5.6M) in 2012.  RMK stated that it will invest 
19.0B roubles (US$627M) in the Chelyabinsk region in 
2012.  Furthermore, the development of a new copper 
wirerod facility at the Cannery Kantemirovsky plant is 
currently being discussed.  The operation would produce approximately 36,000t/y of copper wirerod and would 
require an investment of EUR20-25M. 
European wirerod market stabilises 
Q1 production and consumption in Western Europe appeared weak y-o-y, falling 1.0% and 1.4%, respectively.  
Nonetheless, the region appears to have rebounded from the financial crisis which escalated at the end of Q3 
2011, with production rising 13.7% q-o-q from Q4 2011and consumption up 8.9% for the same period.  From 
Nexans’ Q1 2012 financial report, we can infer that the European wirerod market was supported by a very 
strong automotive sector, driven by demand from German premium auto manufacturers, as well as increased 
infrastructure investment in France and Scandinavia, and a rebounding construction sector in Northern Europe.  
Demand in Southern Europe, meanwhile, continues to be subdued.  Meanwhile, Prysmian reported that 
demand from infrastructure was the most robust in Scandinavia, Eastern Europe and Italy, while the rest of 
Southern Europe was stable.  According to Aurubis, an increase in European demand was evident from recent

Industry News 
Consumption 
• 
The Japanese Electric Wire & Cable Maker’s Association released preliminary figures for 
copper cable shipments in March, which totalled 59,500t, indicating a 5.9% y-o-y increase.  
Copper cable shipments to the automotive sector have shown rapid growth from the previous 
year in each month of Q1 2012, rising by 18.7, 18.9 and 76.2% y-o-y in January, February and 
March 2012 respectively.  The association expect total copper cable shipments to grow by 2.2% 
y-o-y in FY2012 (April-March), with a rise of 3.6% and 2.6% y-o-y anticipated in deliveries to 
the automotive and construction sectors, respectively. 
• 
Wuxi Lineo Science and Technology Group began construction of a 60,000t/y copper wirerod 
mill in Wuxi City, Jiangsu province.  Start-up is expected to take place by October 2012.  The 
company will also invest in a second phase expansion project that will involve the addition of 
another 60,000t/y wirerod production line by November 2014.  The plant will be primarily fed 
with refined copper cathode sourced from Tongling Nonferrous Metals in Anhui province and 
is designed to supply wirerod to domestic wire and cable producers. 
• 
Assomet, the Italian nonferrous semis fabrication association, reported that output of copper and 
copper alloy semi-fabricated products in Italy fell by 4.8% y-o-y to 1.1Mt in 2011.  Copper 
semi-fabricated products output fell by 6.7% to 556,100t in 2011, while copper alloy semis 
production declined by 2.8% to 501,500t.  The association expects the production of copper and 
copper alloy semis to fall by 2.4% in 2012, to 1.0Mt, mainly attributed to poor end-use demand 
caused by increases in housing and value-added taxes.  The association said that orders are 
erratic and that the Italian copper semis production sector is currently operating at 50% capacity 
utilisation, whereas the copper alloy semis sector was slightly higher at 60%. 
• 
The China Household Electrical Appliances Association (CHEAA) said that the Chinese 
government is considering a new round of subsidies for the home appliance sector.  The products 
under consideration are energy-efficient air conditioners and televisions.  The association also 
said that the nation’s inventories of air conditioners stood at 20M units at the end of 2011, 
around twice the normal level. 
• 
Mueller Industries, the US based producer of copper tube and brass products, reported a 
decrease in revenues of 16.0% y-o-y in Q1 2012.  The company attributes this loss to an extra 
week of business in 2011 and to lower raw material costs.  Mueller expects to perform better in 
the remainder of the year as it anticipates a pick-up in US construction.  The company noted that 
building permits for single family homes rose by 30% y-o-y in March 2012 combined with more 
affordable house prices and cheaper mortgages.

Mine Production 
• 
On 16th April, it was reported that production at the Collahuasi mine in Chile will likely fall 
short of its target for 2012 due to 18-20 days of disruption in Q1 from heavy rains and 
snow.  Anglo American said that Collahuasi is unlikely to make up for the loss during the year 
due to declining ore grades.  However, consideration has been given to boosting production by 
accelerating waste removal in order to access higher ore grades earlier.  The 2012 production 
target for the Collahuasi mine is 460,000t of copper-in-concentrate. 
• 
On 21st April, Glencore announced that its majority-owned Zambian subsidiary, Mopani 
Copper Mines, had resumed its operations after a closure due to environmental violations.  The 
company’s Mufulira heap leaching plant was ordered to cease production in March due to 
excessive acid mist emissions.  Last year, Mufulira produced 40,000t of copper-in-concentrate 
and 10,000t of EW cathode. 
• 
On 20th April, it was reported that operations at Milpo’s Ivan copper mine in Chile had been 
suspended as a result of high production costs, which were mainly attributed to declining ore 
grades.  In 2011, the mine produced approximately 6,000t of EW cathode. 
• 
According to Peru’s Mining Federation, Peruvian miners are set to stage a one-day general strike 
on 14th May in protest against dismissals of workers at operations owned by Empresa 
Siderurgica del Peru SAA and Shougang Corp.  The miners are also protesting against the 
proposed shutdown of Renco Group’s zinc smelter. 
• 
A crusher failure occurred at Hillgrove Resources’ Kanmantoo copper mine in Australia.  The 
company reported on 28th March that throughput at the mill had to be reduced by 40,000t/d, 
down to 160,000t/d in March.   Full milling capacity of 200,000t/d is expected to resume in 
April.  The company believes that the lost production can be recovered during the course of 
2012.  Kanmantoo is expected to produce 16,000t of copper-in-concentrate in 2012 and increase 
production to 20,000t in 2013. 
• 
On 3rd April, the Indonesian government announced plans to implement a 25% export tax on 
coal and base metals this year, which may increase to 50% in 2013.  The news comes after 
several announcements of new mining regulations earlier this year, including a ban on exports of 
unprocessed metal ores from 2014.  The latest regulation is intended to prevent a mine 
production boom prior to the 2014 ban coming into force. 
• 
On 30th March, the Zambian government announced plans to phase out the suspension of the 
issuance of mining licences that has been overseen since October 2011.  The suspension was 
imposed in order to root out suspected corruption in the process.  Issuance of rights for 
prospecting as well as mining rights for small scale operations have resumed immediately, but 
the ban on permits remains in place and is expected to be phased out gradually.

The Zambian government announced on the 4th April that it intends to ban the export of copper 
raw materials in an effort to add value to the domestic industry.  The Ministry of Commerce, 
Trade and Industry sees the production of the higher value-added copper and copper products 
as key for reducing unemployment and boosting the local economy.  In 2008, Zambia introduced 
a 15% export levy on copper concentrates aimed at adding value locally.  There are three 
smelters situated in Zambia and in 2011 we estimate that they processed 512,000t of copper-in-
blister with 200,000t of this exported to China for electrorefining.  By comparison, copper-in-
concentrate production amounted to 531,000t in the same period. 
• 
It was reported on 27th April that Oz Minerals remains interested in acquiring Cupru Min SA 
Abrud, which controls the Rosia Poieni mine in Romania.  The company is being sold through 
an ongoing privatisation process administered by the incumbent Romanian government as per an 
agreement made with the International Monetary Fund.  Oz Minerals was a bidder in the sale 
of the company which eventually broke down when the auction winner, Roman Copper 
Corporation, missed a legal deadline to sign the contract agreement.  Roman Copper 
Corporation has since entered into a consortium with Canadian exploration company, Valhalla 
Resources, with the intention of acquiring the Romanian company. 
• 
It was announced on 24th April that CST Mining signed an agreement to sell its 70% stake in the 
Mina Justa copper project in Peru to Cumbres Andinas, a subsidiary of Peru’s Minsur S.A. in 
a deal worth US$505M.  The remaining 30% share is held by Korea’s KORES (15%) and LS 
Nikko Copper (15%).  Upon reaching full capacity, the project is expected to produce 62,000t 
of copper-in-concentrate and 52,000t of EW cathode.  We had expected start-up of the SXEW 
operations in late 2015 followed by commissioning of the concentrator after 2018.  The change 
in ownership may lead to a different development timeframe. 
Exploration and Development 
• 
On 27th April, it was reported that Teck Resources submitted an environmental impact 
assessment for its US$5.6B project to expand the Quebrada Blanca mine in Chile.  The plans 
are aimed at adding production of 200,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate over 39 years.  
Construction is anticipated to begin in July 2013, with commissioning taking place in 2016.  We 
expect production from Quebrada Blanca will total 69,000t of EW cathode in 2012. 
• 
It was reported on 30th April that the Supreme Court of Chile upheld an earlier ruling that the 
environmental permit for Goldcorp's El Morro copper-gold project is invalid.  The ruling was 
made on the grounds that the Chilean environmental permitting authority had not sufficiently 
consulted the indigenous people of an area affected by the project.  Goldcorp, who own a 70% 
stake in the US$3.9B project, has halted development work and does not have a view on how 
long it will take to resolve the environmental issues.  We anticipate that once commissioned the 
project would see production of 170,000t/y of copper-in-concentrate and 9,330kg/y of gold.

Lundin Mining reported on 25th April that the Tenke Fungurume Phase II brownfield 
expansion is on track for start-up in 2013.  Lundin, who owns a 25% stake in the mine, expects 
the US$850M project to see EW cathode production rise by 195,000t/y.  CRU estimates that the 
mine will produce 131,000t of EW cathode in 2012. 
• 
On 29th March, it was announced that KGHM had increased its stake in KGHM Ajax Mining 
from 51% to 80% for US$29.9M.  KGHM Ajax Mining owns the Afton-Ajax copper gold 
project in Canada.  A few days later, KGHM announced that it plans to invest US$795M in the 
project. The construction work is expected to take 2 years and the mine could be operational as 
early as 2015, producing 50,000t of copper-in-concentrate and 2,835kg of gold annually.  
Smelting and Refining 
• 
On 12th April, it was reported that the restructuring plan for Doe Run Peru’s 75,000t/y La 
Oroya smelter was rejected by creditors.  The US$168M investment plans aimed to restore 
operations at the plant after it closed in June 2009 as a result of financial difficulties and a stalled 
environmental cleanup.  Doe Run Peru's main creditor is the Peruvian government, with 36% of 
its debt, while the other major creditor is the Renco Group with 35%.  The plans were rejected 
on the grounds that they potentially rendered the Peruvian government liable for environmental 
lawsuits.  Doe Run Peru has 30 days to revise its restructuring plan before the board is eligible to 
find a new company to operate the plant or liquidate it completely. 
• 
On 10th April, Yunnan Tin said that it expects to meet its goal to begin production of its first 
copper smelter, based in Geiju City, China in mid-2012.  The company expects to produce 
60,000t of copper cathode in 2012, half of the smelter’s 120,000t production capacity.  Copper-
in-concentrate feedstock is expected to be sourced from the overseas market.
